title: Italian Business-to-Business Invoicing Data: A Network Analysis
abstract: We present a comprehensive description of the network of Italian Business-to-Business commercial relationships, based on the universe of electronic invoices collected by the Italian Tax Office. The firm-to-firm detail of the data is exploited to describe the distribution of the numbers of buyers (customers) and sellers (suppliers) per firm, the centrality of each firm in the production network, and the average distance between firms. We characterize for the first time the firm-to-firm network describing the Italian production system, and present its geographic and sectoral breakdown. The analysis reveals heavy tailed distributions for the numbers of buyers and sellers per firm, implying a scale-free structure of the network. The distributions of centrality values display heavy tails as well, indicating a strong concentration of importance in a relatively small number of firms. We estimate the tail exponents for all these distributions, finding in all cases lower exponents for downstream (buyer-side) distributions than for the upstream (seller-side) ones.
summary: This paper analyzes the structure of the Italian B2B commercial network using massive invoicing data, modeling firms as nodes and transactions as weighted edges. It finds the network possesses a scale-free structure and characterizes how economic importance (centrality) is unevenly distributed among a few key firms. The findings offer quantitative insights into the underlying connectivity and vulnerabilities of the national production system.
main_problem: The paper characterizes the structure of the Italian production network using comprehensive firm-to-firm commercial transaction data to derive insights into the Italian economy.
main_result: The network exhibits a scale-free structure, indicated by heavy-tailed distributions for buyer/seller counts and centrality measures. Furthermore, the tail exponents for buyer-side distributions are found to be lower than those for seller-side distributions.
method: Network analysis techniques are employed, treating firms as nodes and invoices as weighted, directed edges. Key metrics analyzed include degree distributions, network centrality (Eigenvector, Katz, PageRank), and structural properties like assortativity.
model_or_system: The system is the network of Italian Business-to-Business (B2B) commercial relationships, constructed from electronic invoicing data from the Italian Tax Office. Nodes are firms, and edges are weighted by the total monetary amount exchanged.
key_observables: Distribution of buyers/sellers per firm, network centrality measures, tail exponents of degree distributions, network density, and mean degree.
important_parameters: The analysis is based on the 2019 Italian electronic invoicing data, focusing on the B2B subset of transactions.
main_assumptions: The analysis is static, and while the data coverage is comprehensive, the comparison of network metrics across different international datasets is cautioned against due to potential methodological variations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the flow of transactions between entity types, the number of firms per economic sector (NACE), and maps showing regional/sectoral variations in centrality measures. Tables compare network metrics across different countries.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the economic importance of micro-structure, details the unique B2B dataset, analyzes fundamental network statistics (scale-free, small-world), and concludes with detailed sectoral and geographical breakdowns of centrality.
why_interesting: The application of complex network theory, which shares mathematical tools with statistical physics (e.g., power-law distributions, critical phenomena), to a real-world economic system provides a model for analyzing emergent collective behavior in non-physical systems.
